angle.title: One Payment, Two Verdicts
angle.logline: A cabinet secretary was convicted of accepting a $100,000 bribe; the oilman who sent him the money was acquitted of giving it. The court record explains how both verdicts came to stand.
angle.centralQuestion: How could one jury convict Fall of taking Doheny's $100,000 as a bribe while another acquitted Doheny of giving it?
angle.whyItWorks: The contrast is real, documented, and counter-intuitive, so tension comes from the record itself. It also forces the precision the case demands: civil findings vs. criminal verdicts, and each man's own trial.
risks: Blurring civil fraud findings into criminal guilt for Doheny or Sinclair — every civil finding is attributed to the court that made it.
Viewers may hear the two verdicts as a contradiction; the AP-reported jury instruction (each verdict was possible) must be included.
The Fall–Doheny conspiracy verdict date is not in the record; it is narrated without a date.

alternativeAngles.title: The Shadowed Jury
alternativeAngles.logline: Harry Sinclair's conspiracy trial collapsed when he had detectives follow the jurors; he went to prison for contempt, yet was acquitted of the conspiracy itself.
alternativeAngles.centralQuestion: How did the man at the center of Teapot Dome end up imprisoned for contempt but acquitted of conspiracy?
alternativeAngles.whyItWorks: A strong, primary-sourced turning point with a clear courtroom arc.
risks: Sidelines the $100,000 and Fall's conviction, the best-documented outcome.
Whether and when Sinclair served his sentences is an open question.

alternativeAngles.title: Follow the Bonds
alternativeAngles.logline: Liberty Bonds traced by serial number from a shell company to Fall's son-in-law — and a money trail that ends in destroyed records and silent witnesses.
alternativeAngles.centralQuestion: Where did the bonds come from, and why could no one say?
alternativeAngles.whyItWorks: A strong document detail with genuine mystery.
risks: The central question (who owned Continental Trading) is UNRESOLVABLE in this record — the angle would end on a gap.
Risk of implying guilt from witnesses invoking a legal privilege.

hook.description: Open on the documented delivery of $100,000 in cash (November 30, 1921), then state the two opposite verdicts about that same money. No rhetorical question in the hook; the contrast carries it.

centralQuestion: How could one jury convict Fall of taking Doheny's $100,000 as a bribe while another acquitted Doheny of giving it?

sequences.title: The Cash
sequences.purpose: Establish the single payment and the two opposite verdicts, so the viewer watches for how both happened.

beats.description: Doheny's son carries $100,000 in cash from New York to Washington and gives it to Fall.
One jury convicts Fall of accepting it as a bribe; another acquits Doheny of giving it.

sequences.title: The Navy's Oil
sequences.purpose: Explain the reserves and how Fall came to control their leasing — briefly.

beats.description: Teapot Dome set aside in 1915 as Naval Petroleum Reserve No. 3.
Fall takes office (March 1921); Harding's executive order puts the reserves under Interior (May 1921).
Supreme Court: Fall keen to control leasing. Fall's July 1921 letter to Doheny: 'exactly as I think best.'

sequences.title: Two Leases
sequences.purpose: The money and the leases, in date order: Doheny's cash and Elk Hills, then Sinclair and Teapot Dome. Present the loan/bribe dispute as competing positions.

beats.description: The $100,000: Doheny said loan, the government said bribe; per the court findings, Doheny later tore Fall's signature off the note.
Elk Hills lease to Doheny's company, without competition; secrecy agreed with Admiral Robison (per court findings).
Sinclair visits Fall's ranch, proposes the lease, organizes Mammoth Oil; the Teapot Dome lease is signed April 7, 1922 and kept secret.

sequences.title: The Money Trail
sequences.purpose: The Senate investigation: Fall's denial, the bonds, the silent witnesses, Sinclair's refusal. Plant Fall's denial and Sinclair's refusal for later payoffs.

beats.description: Senate authorizes the investigation (April 1922).
Fall leaves office; Sinclair gives him $25,000 in bonds; Sinclair's counsel testifies it was a loan.
Fall's December 1923 letter: not 'one cent on account of any oil lease'; his McLean explanation, which McLean denied.
Liberty Bonds traced to Continental Trading; records destroyed; witnesses invoke privilege or refuse to testify (no inference of guilt).
Sinclair refuses to answer the committee, reserving his evidence 'for those courts.'

sequences.title: The Civil Track
sequences.purpose: The courts cancel the leases — and expressly do not decide the bribery question for Teapot Dome. Draw the civil/criminal line out loud.

beats.description: Teapot Dome civil suit: trial court finds no fraud; appeals court reverses.
Supreme Court 1927: Elk Hills consummated by conspiracy, corruption and fraud; Teapot Dome lease fraudulent, cancelled.
The Court states it is not deciding whether Fall was bribed over Teapot Dome. These are civil rulings, not criminal verdicts.

sequences.title: The Criminal Track
sequences.purpose: Conspiracy acquittals, the shadowed jury, contempt convictions (and the Burns reversal), Sinclair's acquittal, and his Senate contempt conviction.

beats.description: Fall and Doheny accused together of conspiracy (May 1925); both acquitted (date not in record).
October 1927 trial; Burns detectives shadow the jurors on Sinclair's authorization; Sinclair's stated justification; no juror shown to have been approached; mistrial.
Contempt of court: Sinclair, Day, W. Sherman Burns convicted and affirmed; William J. Burns convicted then reversed.
Fall severed for poor health; Sinclair acquitted April 21, 1928; separately, Senate contempt conviction affirmed.

sequences.title: Two Verdicts
sequences.purpose: Pay off the hook: Fall's bribery trial and conviction, Doheny's acquittal, and the reported jury instruction that makes both verdicts possible.

beats.description: Fall in a wheelchair; his own counsel's 'deliberately lied' argument in full; the judge: not on trial for lying.
Fall convicted of bribery; $100,000 fine and one year.
Doheny acquitted March 22, 1930; AP: jury accepted the loan position; judge's reported instruction that both outcomes were possible.
As of March 1930 Fall had not gone to jail; conviction affirmed April 6, 1931.

sequences.title: What the Record Says
sequences.purpose: Answer the central question honestly per man, restate the Teapot Dome non-finding, and name what this record does not settle.

beats.description: For Fall, yes (convicted, affirmed); for Doheny, no (acquitted); on Teapot Dome, the Supreme Court did not decide.
Not settled in this record: whether/when Fall served his sentence; who stood behind Continental Trading.

reveals.description: The hook states the opposite verdicts; the full trials and the reported jury instruction explaining how both could stand are delivered in the verdicts sequence.
Fall's 1923 denial of receiving 'one cent' is planted in the money trail; at his bribery trial his own counsel argues he deliberately lied to the Senate (with the full continuation).
Sinclair reserves his evidence 'for those courts'; in court, his trial collapses over the jury he had shadowed.
After the secret Teapot Dome lease is set up, the Supreme Court cancels it as fraudulent yet expressly declines to decide whether Fall was bribed over it.

pacing.notes: Script estimate is about 561s at 150 wpm (case target 480s, within the 20% tolerance). The criminal track is the longest sequence because it carries the most legal outcomes; background is kept under 40s. Final timing comes from measured narration after Gate 2a.

endingStrategy.description: Answer the central question per man as the courts did — Fall convicted and affirmed, Doheny acquitted — restate that the Supreme Court did not decide the Teapot Dome bribery question, and say plainly what this record leaves open.
